description: A service processes requests and persists results. Under most conditions, each request produces a single persisted record. However, under certain execution sequences, multiple records can appear that correspond to what seems to be the same logical operation. The issue is intermittent and depends on execution ordering and prior activity. Individual components appear correct when inspected in isolation: the persistence layer correctly appends records, and request handling produces deterministic results. The inconsistency only emerges under specific multi-step flows.
task:
A system processes requests and writes results to persistent storage.

In most cases, each request results in a single stored record. However, under certain sequences of operations, multiple records may be produced that appear to correspond to the same logical request.

The issue is not consistently reproducible and seems sensitive to prior operations and execution ordering. The persistence layer appears to behave correctly, and request processing logic appears deterministic when examined independently.

Identify the root cause of the duplication and refactor the implementation so that each logical request produces at most one persisted result, without removing append-only behavior from storage and without introducing global deduplication mechanisms.
trap: Several fixes appear to resolve the issue under limited testing: (1) deduplicating records in storage by request_id, (2) caching processed request_ids at the service entry point, or (3) preventing repeated writes when the same request is observed. These approaches succeed in simple scenarios but fail under specific execution sequences because the identity used for persistence is not stable across all execution paths and the write-producing path can be re-entered in ways that bypass these guards.

ground_truth_bug.invariant: Each logical request must produce at most one persisted result regardless of execution ordering
ground_truth_bug.fix_pattern: Ensure the write-producing path is idempotent per logical request by stabilizing identity and preventing duplicate side effects across re-entry

oracle_ground_truth.bug_type: hidden retry-induced double execution with identity drift
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_source: The write-producing path can be re-entered under certain execution sequences after the result has already been persisted, and the identity used for persistence is recomputed or transformed such that repeated executions are not recognized as duplicates
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_property: Multiple executions of the same logical operation can produce distinct persistence identities, allowing duplicate records to accumulate
mechanism_steps: A request is processed and produces a result that is written to storage
An execution path re-enters the same processing logic for what is logically the same request
The identity used for persistence is recomputed or transformed across executions
The system does not recognize the second execution as equivalent to the first
A second write occurs, producing another persisted record
Duplicate records accumulate for what is logically the same request
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_outcome: Multiple persisted records correspond to a single logical request under certain execution sequences
oracle_ground_truth.trap_description: Local deduplication or caching fixes appear to work but fail because identity is not stable across executions and the write path can be re-entered after side effects have already occurred

description: A user profile object maintains raw identity fields together with multiple presentation-oriented representations used by different access paths. Most reads appear correct, and formatting helpers behave correctly in isolation. However, after certain update sequences, different consumers of the same profile can observe different display values even though the underlying base fields were updated successfully. The failure is subtle because some read paths compute from current base fields while others consume cached or serialized presentation state.
task:
A user model stores core identity fields and also supports several user-facing representations used by different methods.

After updating a user's name, some reads reflect the new values while other reads continue to expose an older presentation of the same user. The issue is intermittent in the sense that it depends on which read path was exercised before and after the update. No exceptions are raised, and the formatting logic appears correct when tested directly.

Identify the root cause of the inconsistency and refactor the implementation so that all externally visible representations of a user remain consistent after updates, without removing caching entirely, without changing external method signatures, and without moving formatting logic out of the module.
trap: Several locally plausible fixes exist: (1) recomputing only the top-level display field inside update_name, (2) changing a read method to always call the formatter dynamically, (3) clearing one cached presentation value but leaving others intact, or (4) modifying the formatter itself. Each of these appears to fix one observation path, but they fail because multiple externally visible representations are derived from shared base state through different code paths, and only part of that derived state is refreshed after mutation.

ground_truth_bug.invariant: All externally observable representations derived from a user's identity fields must stay mutually consistent after any successful mutation
ground_truth_bug.fix_pattern: Centralize derived-state refresh or invalidation so every identity-dependent cached or serialized representation is updated consistently whenever base identity fields change

oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_source: The object maintains more than one identity-derived representation, and update_name refreshes base fields plus only a subset of those derived representations
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_property: Different read paths observe different representations of the same user because some values are recomputed from current state while others continue to serve stale cached or serialized identity data
mechanism_steps: The user object is initialized with base identity fields and multiple derived presentation representations
At least one read path returns data derived dynamically from current base fields
At least one other read path returns cached or precomputed presentation state
update_name mutates the base identity fields successfully
update_name refreshes only part of the identity-derived state, leaving another representation stale
Subsequent reads diverge depending on which accessor or serialization path is used
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_outcome: The same logical user is exposed with inconsistent outward-facing identity data across access paths after mutation
oracle_ground_truth.trap_description: A shallow fix that updates one display field or one accessor appears correct under narrow testing, but the real issue is incomplete synchronization of multiple derived identity representations

description: A request pipeline resolves a policy version, prepares a compatibility-adjusted execution context, and executes behavior based on both. In isolation, each stage appears correct: resolution returns the expected version, compatibility logic conditionally modifies context, and execution branches on the provided version and flags. However, under certain multi-request sequences, execution follows fallback behavior even though resolution reports a valid non-fallback version. The discrepancy is intermittent and depends on prior requests and how context evolves across stages.
task:
A system processes requests through three stages: version resolution, compatibility adjustment, and execution.

In most cases, execution behavior matches the resolved version. However, under certain sequences of requests, execution follows fallback behavior even when resolution reports a valid version.

The issue is not tied to a single input and appears only after specific prior requests have been processed. Each stage appears locally correct when inspected independently.

Identify the root cause of the inconsistency and refactor the implementation so that execution behavior always reflects the resolved version for each request, while preserving compatibility behavior and without introducing global resets or disabling fallback logic.
trap: Multiple plausible fixes exist and each appears correct under partial testing: (1) forcing executor to rely only on the resolved version, (2) tightening fallback conditions, (3) reconstructing the top-level context per request, or (4) normalizing version fields earlier. These fixes can eliminate the issue for simple cases but fail under specific request sequences because they do not address how identity and compatibility state drift across stages.

from typing import Dict, Any


def normalize_context(ctx: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    compat = ctx.get("compat", {})
    flags = compat.get("flags", {})

    # Derive normalized execution view
    normalized = {
        "version": ctx["resolved_version"],
        "use_fallback": flags.get("force_fallback", False),
        "mode": "compat" if flags.get("compat_mode") else "strict",
    }

    return normalized

from typing import Dict, Any

from compat import attach_compatibility_context
from normalizer import normalize_context


def resolve_version(request: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    # Deterministic resolution (correct)
    if request.get("use_legacy"):
        return "legacy_v1"
    return "v2"


def execute(request: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    ctx: Dict[str, Any] = {}

    # Stage 1: resolve
    ctx["resolved_version"] = resolve_version(request)

    # Stage 2: attach compatibility
    ctx = attach_compatibility_context(ctx)

    # Stage 3: normalize for execution
    norm = normalize_context(ctx)

    # Stage 4: execute
    if norm["use_fallback"]:
        return f"fallback:{norm['version']}"
    return f"primary:{norm['version']}"

ground_truth_bug.invariant: The execution decision must be derived from a stable, per-request representation of version and compatibility state
ground_truth_bug.fix_pattern: Ensure per-request isolation and stable identity by eliminating shared mutable nested structures and preventing cross-stage mutation of identity-relevant fields

oracle_ground_truth.bug_type: cross-stage identity drift with shared mutation
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_source: A nested compatibility structure is reused across requests and is further transformed by a normalization step, causing identity-relevant fields to drift across stages and across requests
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_property: Execution reads a representation of version/compatibility that has been mutated by prior requests and altered by intermediate normalization, leading to divergence from the originally resolved version
mechanism_steps: Resolver produces a correct version identifier for the current request
Compatibility layer attaches a context that reuses a nested mutable structure shared across requests
A prior request mutates compatibility-related flags in this shared structure (e.g., enabling fallback conditions)
Normalizer transforms or reorders fields in the context, creating a derived representation used by executor
The current request inherits mutated compatibility state through the shared structure
Executor reads the normalized context and evaluates fallback conditions based on mutated state rather than the current request's resolution
Execution follows fallback behavior even though the resolver returned a valid version
oracle_ground_truth.mechanism_outcome: Execution behavior diverges from resolved policy due to cross-request state leakage combined with representation drift across stages
oracle_ground_truth.trap_description: Local fixes in executor or resolver appear to correct the issue but fail because the root cause spans compatibility state reuse and transformation across stages
